631.title: The whirlpool ahead
631.hook: a man swept downstream, warned by someone on the bank
631.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use river and flood images for craving, and many describe the teacher's role, as here, as someone on the bank who can see dangers the practitioner cannot yet see.

segments.voice: Yesterday: conscience and concern, and your line, two bright guardians. Did you listen to one small don't? Today, a warning from outside, shouted from a riverbank. Day six hundred thirty-one.

Floating down a lazy river on a summer afternoon is one of life's easy pleasures. Warm water, sun on your face, the current doing all the work. You don't have to decide anything. That's the picture at the start of one of the last teachings in the Itivuttaka. A man is being carried along by a river that looks lovely and pleasant. He's enjoying it. And then someone standing on the bank, someone who can see further down than he can, starts shouting. Today: the whirlpool ahead.
screen: `A LAZY RIVER, A SUMMER AFTERNOON.` → `THE CURRENT DOES THE WORK.` → `SOMEONE ON THE BANK SHOUTS.`

segments.voice: Hey, the man on the bank calls. You're being carried along by a river that looks pleasant. But downstream there's a pool with waves and whirlpools, with dangerous creatures in it. If you reach it, you'll come to grief. And the man in the water, hearing that, struggles against the current with his hands and feet. Then the Buddha explains the picture, piece by piece. The river's current is craving. The pleasant, alluring look of it is your own six senses, how good it all seems through them. The pool downstream stands for the five lower fetters, the ties that bind beings to this world. The waves are anger and despair. The whirlpools are the five strands of sense pleasure, the pull of sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches. Turning against the stream is renunciation. Struggling with hands and feet is effort. And the one standing on the bank, who can see what the swimmer can't? That, the Buddha says, is the one who has awakened. You may remember a swimmer from earlier this year, with four dangers in the water: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, sharks. Today the river adds something: the danger doesn't look dangerous. It looks like a nice afternoon. That's why the warning matters. You can't see the whirlpool from the water. You need someone on the bank. And the swimmer in the story does the one thing that counts: he hears, and he turns.
screen: `A RIVER THAT LOOKS PLEASANT.` · `A POOL WITH WAVES AND WHIRLPOOLS.` · `THE CURRENT IS CRAVING.` · `THE ONE ON THE BANK CAN SEE.` · then, large: `THE WHIRLPOOL AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: heed one warning. Sit and settle. Think of a warning someone has given you lately, gently or not: a friend, a doctor, a parent, even your own body. Maybe you nodded and kept floating. Picture them on the bank, calling. What can they see that you can't from the water? You don't have to swim hard yet. Just turn your head toward the bank and listen. The bell holds the time.
The whirlpool ahead. In the Itivuttaka, a man carried by a pleasant river is warned from the bank of the whirlpools downstream, and turns. Today's word.
Your line: the whirlpool ahead. Today, take one warning seriously that you've been floating past, and make one small stroke toward the bank. Day six hundred thirty-one.

options: keep floating; it feels fine.

fork.reveal: he hears and turns, working against the current. the Buddha says that struggle is effort, and the one on the bank is the awakened one.

what a scholar hears: Iti 109 (Nadisota Sutta) glosses each element of the simile, and the image parallels the swimmer's dangers of MN 67.

632.title: First teachers
632.hook: parents are called first teachers, worthy of honor (Itivuttaka 106)
632.howItsDone: In many Buddhist households, especially in Theravada countries, children bow to their parents on special days, and families make offerings or give food to monks in their parents' names as a way of honoring them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a man drifting downstream, a voice from the bank, and your line, the whirlpool ahead. Did you heed one warning? Today the Itivuttaka turns from the river to the family home. Day six hundred thirty-two.

Who taught you to hold a spoon? Nobody remembers the lesson, but somebody gave it, probably more than once, probably with a towel nearby. Before any school, any book, any teacher with a title, there was a pair of hands showing you how the world works: this is hot, this is a cat, this is how you say thank you. One short discourse in the Itivuttaka gives those hands a name. It calls them by a title usually kept for honored teachers. Today: first teachers.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO HOLD A SPOON?` → `BEFORE ANY SCHOOL.` → `A TITLE FOR THOSE HANDS.`

segments.voice: The discourse is Itivuttaka 106. The Buddha says that a family where mother and father are honored at home lives with Brahma, the high god of that world. It lives with the first teachers. It lives with those worthy of gifts. Then he unpacks each name. Brahma, first teachers, worthy of gifts: these, he says, are terms for mother and father. And he gives the reason in one plain sentence, paraphrased here: parents do much for their children. They bring them up, they feed them, and they show them this world. Show them this world. That's the job description of a first teacher. Not doctrine, not scripture. The world itself: a face, a word, a door, a road. The Pali for first teachers is pubbacariya, from pubba, earlier or first, and acariya, a teacher. In the Buddha's day an acariya was a figure of real respect, someone you served and thanked. Here the title goes to the people in the kitchen. The verse at the end gets practical. The wise honor them with food and drink, with clothes and a place to sleep, by bathing them and washing their feet. Care for the body that once cared for yours. Two honest things belong beside this text. First, it speaks of parents as they are meant to be, the ones who raise, feed and show. Not everyone had that, and the text doesn't pretend to describe every home. Many Buddhist teachers widen it to whoever did that work for you: a grandmother, an aunt, a neighbor, a foster parent. Second, the same idea runs through the Buddha's teaching to Sigala, where a grown child supports the parents who once supported them. Honor, here, isn't a feeling first. It's food, clothing, a place to rest.
screen: `MOTHER AND FATHER, HONORED AT HOME` · `THEY SHOW THEIR CHILDREN THIS WORLD` · `PUBBACARIYA: TEACHER FROM THE START` · `FOOD, CLOTHES, A PLACE TO REST` · then, large: `FIRST TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one person who showed you this world when you were small. A parent, if that's who it was, or a grandparent, an elder, anyone who fed you and named things for you. Picture one ordinary thing they taught you, the spoon, the shoelace, the way to say sorry. Stay with that picture and let a quiet thank you sit in the chest. If they're living, after the bell you might send them a short message. If they're gone, the thanks can stay right here. The bell holds the time.
First teachers. Pubbacariya: in Itivuttaka 106, a name for mother and father, who raise, feed, and show their children this world. Today's word.
Your line: first teachers. Thank one parent or elder today for one small thing they taught you, in a call, a note, or just in your head. Day six hundred thirty-two.

what a scholar hears: the same sutta, calling parents Brahma, first teachers and worthy of gifts, appears in the Anguttara Nikaya too; since Brahma was revered as a high god in the brahmin tradition, many readers see the title as moving sacred honor into the household.

633.title: In every posture
633.hook: walking, standing, sitting, lying down, keep effort alive (Itivuttaka 110)
633.howItsDone: Many Buddhist teachers include walking meditation alongside sitting, and some monastic training asks students to keep mindfulness through all four postures, from walking and standing to sitting and lying down.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parents called by a teacher's title, and your line, first teachers. Did you thank someone? Today the Itivuttaka follows you through the day, from your feet to your pillow. Day six hundred thirty-three.

Walking to the bus, a grudge shows up. Standing in line for coffee, it's still there. Sitting at your desk, you polish it. Lying in bed at night, you rehearse what you should have said. Four positions, one thought, carried all day like a stone in a shoe. The body changes posture a hundred times a day. The mind often doesn't. One discourse near the end of the Itivuttaka walks through exactly those four positions and asks what you do with a thought like that in each one. Today: in every posture.
screen: `A GRUDGE AT THE BUS STOP.` → `STILL THERE IN BED.` → `FOUR POSTURES, ONE THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Itivuttaka 110 is built like a walk through the day. If, while a monk is walking, a thought of sensual craving, ill will, or harming arises, and he puts up with it, doesn't drop it, doesn't drive it out, then, the Buddha says, he is called lazy, lacking ardor. Then the same sentence again for standing. Again for sitting. Again for lying down awake. Four times, nearly word for word. Then the other side, four times over. If the thought arises while walking and he doesn't tolerate it, but lets it go, dispels it, ends it, he is called ardent, someone whose effort is alive. The Pali tradition counts these four, walking, standing, sitting and lying down, as the four postures, iriyapatha, literally ways of moving. Other suttas use them to say all the time, the whole day and night. Notice what the text does not say. It doesn't say the thought shouldn't arise. Thoughts of wanting, of anger, of hurting someone come to everyone, monks included. The line is drawn after: do you tolerate it, feed it, let it settle in, or do you see it and set it down? That's a very different standard from never having the thought at all. And notice why the list is so repetitive. Practice isn't only for the cushion. A sitting meditator who spends the walk home nursing a grudge has done one posture out of four. The verse at the end pictures a person like that as someone who keeps at it, walking or standing, sitting or lying down, and the text says such a one can reach the highest awakening.
screen: `WALKING, STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN` · `PUTTING UP WITH IT, OR LETTING IT GO` · `THE THOUGHT ISN'T THE PROBLEM` · `NOT ONLY ON THE CUSHION` · then, large: `IN EVERY POSTURE.`

segments.voice: Notice how you're sitting right now. Feel the weight in the seat, the feet on the floor, the hands. Let the spine lift a little, without strain. Then check the mind the same way: is anything being carried, a worry, a grudge, a wanting? If something is there, don't fight it. Just see it, the way you saw your posture, and loosen your grip on it a little, the way you loosened your shoulders. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
In every posture. Walking, standing, sitting, lying down: Itivuttaka 110 asks you not to tolerate harmful thoughts in any of the four, and calls that effort alive. Today's word.
Your line: in every posture. Each time you change position today, standing up, sitting down, lying down tonight, check once: what am I carrying? Day six hundred thirty-three.

fork.reveal: the text doesn't fault the arising. it calls you ardent for not tolerating it, right there, in whatever posture you're in.

trapdoor: what you thought: in every posture means sitting up straight.

what a scholar hears: the four iriyapatha recur across the canon, from the posture section of the mindfulness discourses to verses like this one, as shorthand for the whole of waking life.

634.title: As he speaks, he does
634.hook: the Tathagata does as he says and says as he does (Itivuttaka 112)
634.carry: as he speaks, so he does
634.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions take the Buddha's consistency of word and deed as a model; monastics in many places recite the rules of training together regularly, partly so that what they say they keep is matched by what they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and your line, in every posture. What were you carrying? Today, the last discourse of the Itivuttaka, and a name explained. Day six hundred thirty-four.

A coach yells at players to stay calm, red in the face. A parent says put the phone away, while scrolling. A friend swears they'll be on time, again. Nobody needs a lecture on hypocrisy; we all spot the gap between saying and doing in about half a second, usually faster in other people than in ourselves. The Itivuttaka's very last discourse names one person in whom, it says, the gap isn't there at all, and it builds one of his titles out of that. Today: as he speaks, he does.
screen: `CALM DOWN, SHOUTED.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN SAYING AND DOING.` → `THE LAST DISCOURSE.`

segments.voice: Itivuttaka 112 lists reasons the Buddha is called Tathagata, a title he often uses for himself. The word can be read as thus-gone or thus-come, and the discourse plays with it. He has fully understood the world, its arising, its ending, and the way to its ending. From the night of his awakening to the night of his final passing, whatever he says is so and not otherwise. And then the line for today. In Pali it has a lovely rhythm: yathavadi tathakari, yathakari tathavadi. As he says, so he does. As he does, so he says. Notice it runs both directions. Plenty of people do what they say, eventually. Fewer say only what they actually do, no padding, no spin, no talking themselves up. The sutta wants both: the deed matches the word, and the word matches the deed. That's why, it says, he is called Tathagata, the one who is thus. There's a practical side to this for anyone who isn't a Buddha. Elsewhere the texts tell the story of the Buddha's teaching to his son Rahula: before you act, while you act, after you act, look at it. Does it match? A life where words and deeds line up has one big advantage: there's nothing to keep track of. No cover stories, no two versions. And it's the end of a collection. The Itivuttaka began, more than a hundred discourses ago, with this was said by the Blessed One. It closes with a picture of someone whose saying and doing are the same thing.
screen: `WHY HE IS CALLED TATHAGATA` · `WHATEVER HE SAYS IS SO` · `AS HE SAYS, SO HE DOES, AND BACK` · `NOTHING TO KEEP TRACK OF` · then, large: `AS HE SPEAKS, SO HE DOES.`

segments.voice: Settle in and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've said lately that you meant: I'll call, I'll help, I'll rest more, I'll stop doing that. Pick just one. Hold it lightly. Now picture the deed that would match it, as small and specific as you can: the call at six, the ten minutes of help, the phone left in the other room. See yourself doing it. Let the word and the deed sit side by side, until they feel like one thing. The bell holds the time.
As he speaks. Yathavadi tathakari: as he says, so he does, and as he does, so he says. Itivuttaka 112's reason the Buddha is called Tathagata. Today's word.
Your line: as he speaks, so he does. Match one word you've said with one deed today, even a small one, and notice how it feels to have nothing to explain. Day six hundred thirty-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: as he speaks, he does is a saying about keeping promises.

635.title: The short books, closed
635.hook: the Sutta Nipata, the Udana, the Itivuttaka
635.howItsDone: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, such as the discourse on kindness, the jewel discourse and the highest blessings, are among the texts Theravada communities chant regularly, and many Buddhists learn short sayings from these books by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Itivuttaka's last discourse, and your line, as he speaks, so he does. Did a word and a deed line up? Today we close the short books, sixty days of them, and look back. Day six hundred thirty-five.

Some of the best things people say are short. A grandparent's one line at a wedding. A note left on the fridge. A verse someone copied onto a card and kept in a wallet for thirty years. The last sixty days lived in books like that. Not the long discourses, with their journeys and debates, but three small collections of verses and sayings, some of them only a few lines long. They're shelved together in the Pali canon's Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of short texts. Today we close them. Today: the short books.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `A VERSE KEPT IN A WALLET.` → `SIXTY DAYS OF SHORT BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the Sutta Nipata, which many scholars count among the oldest Buddhist poetry we have. It opened with a monk shedding the world like a snake sheds its skin. We walked alone like the rhinoceros horn, or with a good friend. We read the discourse on kindness again, the jewel discourse, and the highest blessings, from caring for parents to a mind unshaken. A boat, the dart of grief, the chapter of eights, and the long road to the far shore. Second, the Udana, inspired sayings, words the Buddha spoke when something moved him. In the seen, only the seen. Boys tormenting fish. The blind men each holding a part of the elephant. And the rare, quiet line, there is an unborn. Third, the Itivuttaka, thus it was said: sayings remembered, the tradition says, by a woman who heard them and repeated them for others. Share even the last bite. Two bright guardians, conscience and concern. The whirlpool ahead. Parents as first teachers. Effort in every posture. And word and deed made one. What do the three books share? They're compact. A whole teaching fits in a breath or two. That's why people memorized them, chanted them, and still do. And they're not shallow for being short. Short sayings ask more of the listener. A long discourse explains itself. A short verse leaves room, and you have to step into it. Tomorrow a very different kind of book begins, thousands of discourses sorted by subject. The short books stay on the shelf, ready.
screen: `THE SUTTA NIPATA: OLD POEMS` · `THE UDANA: INSPIRED SAYINGS` · `THE ITIVUTTAKA: THUS IT WAS SAID` · `SHORT SAYINGS ASK MORE OF YOU` · then, large: `SHORT AND DEEP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the last sixty days drift past: the snake's skin, the rhinoceros, the jewel, the boat, the elephant, the whirlpool, the first teachers. Don't try to remember them all. Wait for one to stay. Whichever comes back on its own, that's your favorite, at least today. Let it sit in the mind, and say its line quietly to yourself, as short as you can make it. Breathe with it. After the bell, if you like, go back and reread it. The bell holds the time.
The short books. The Sutta Nipata, the Udana and the Itivuttaka, three small collections of verse and saying from the Khuddaka Nikaya: short, and deep. Today's word.
Your line: short and deep. Carry one short line from these sixty days with you today, and say it once when you need it. Day six hundred thirty-five.

what a scholar hears: parts of the Sutta Nipata, especially the chapter of eights and the way to the far shore, are often counted among the oldest strata of the canon; the Itivuttaka's frame story credits the laywoman Khujjuttara.

636.title: The Connected Sayings
636.hook: thousands of short discourses gathered by topic
636.howItsDone: Theravada monastics and lay students study the Samyutta Nikaya chapter by chapter, and teachers often draw short similes from it for talks, since its discourses are grouped by topic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the short books closed, and your line, short and deep. Which line stayed with you? Today a new block begins, and a very different kind of book: thousands of discourses, sorted like a library. Day six hundred thirty-six.

Picture a kitchen drawer where everything goes in together: batteries, rubber bands, birthday candles, a screwdriver. You know what's in there, but finding any one thing takes a while. Now picture the same things sorted into small labeled boxes. Candles here. Batteries there. Same things, completely different drawer. The early Buddhist community had thousands of short teachings to remember, and at some point someone sorted a great many of them into boxes by topic. That sorted drawer is the third great collection of the Pali canon. Today: the Samyutta Nikaya.
screen: `A DRAWER OF EVERYTHING.` → `NOW SORT IT INTO BOXES.` → `THOUSANDS OF TEACHINGS, BY TOPIC.`

segments.voice: Samyutta means connected, or yoked together, and nikaya means a collection. So the Connected Sayings: discourses yoked together by their subject. The Long Discourses were sorted by length. The Middle-Length, more or less by length too. The Samyutta is sorted by kind. All the conversations with devas go in one chapter. All the meetings with Mara in another. The talks with King Pasenadi together, the teachings on feeling together, on the five heaps, on the six senses, on the path. There are fifty-six of these chapters, gathered into five books. The first book is the one with verses, full of short poems and questions from gods, kings and nuns. The others take on the great themes: how things arise from causes, the heaps, the senses, and finally the path and the four noble truths. Many of the discourses are tiny, a few lines, sometimes just a simile. That's what makes the collection so useful to read slowly. Here's one, paraphrased, from the chapter on breakthrough. The Buddha picks up a little dust on the tip of his fingernail and asks the monks: which is more, this dust or the great earth? The earth, sir, of course. The dust is nothing beside it. In the same way, he says, for a disciple who has truly seen the teaching, the suffering already ended is like the earth. What's left is like the dust on a fingernail. That's the whole discourse. The Connected Sayings are full of moments like that, small, sorted, and easy to find again. For the next weeks, we'll open the boxes one at a time.
screen: `SAMYUTTA: YOKED TOGETHER` · `SORTED BY KIND, NOT LENGTH` · `FIFTY-SIX CHAPTERS, FIVE BOOKS` · `DUST ON A FINGERNAIL` · then, large: `GATHERED BY KIND.`

segments.voice: Here's a short discourse to read with the body. Hold up one hand and look at a fingernail. Imagine a few grains of dust on its tip. Then let the mind open out to the ground under you, the street, the land, the whole earth. Feel the difference in size. Now think of a difficulty you've already come through in life, something that once felt enormous and is behind you. Let it be the earth. Whatever is still hard today, let it, for now, be the dust. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Samyutta Nikaya. The Connected Sayings: thousands of short discourses, yoked together by topic into fifty-six chapters and five books. Today's word.
Your line: gathered by kind. Read one short discourse today, from any book you like, and notice what kind of box it would belong in. Day six hundred thirty-six.

637.title: Crossing the flood
637.hook: how did you cross? by not halting and not straining (SN 1.1)
637.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions describe balanced effort as neither too tight nor too loose, and the first discourse of the Samyutta Nikaya is often cited when they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Samyutta Nikaya opened, thousands of short discourses, and your line, gathered by kind. Did you read one? Today we read its very first, and close a week. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

Late at night, a glow fills the Jeta Grove near Savatthi. A deva, a radiant being from the heavens, has come down to see the Buddha. It bows, stands to one side, and asks one question, the question that opens the whole Connected Sayings. How, dear sir, did you cross the flood? The flood, in these texts, is everything that sweeps a person along: wanting, becoming, views, not knowing. The answer is a handful of words in Pali, and it sounds like a riddle. Today: crossing the flood.
screen: `A GLOW IN THE JETA GROVE.` → `HOW DID YOU CROSS THE FLOOD?` → `AN ANSWER LIKE A RIDDLE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers: by not halting, friend, and by not straining, I crossed the flood. The deva asks the obvious thing: how? He explains. When I stood still, I sank. When I pushed hard, I was swept away. So, not halting and not straining, I crossed. Picture a swimmer in a strong river. Stop moving and you go under. Thrash and fight the current and you wear yourself out and get carried off anyway. What gets you across is steady movement, without either. The Buddhist tradition reads this in many ways. Some commentators say halting means getting stuck in craving and views, and straining means getting carried away by them. Others hear it as the middle way of the very first sermon, between indulgence and harsh effort. Many meditation teachers just hear practical advice: don't quit, don't force. The deva is delighted. It speaks a verse: after a long time, at last, I see a brahmin, a holy one, fully at peace, who without halting, without straining, has crossed over clinging to the world. Then it bows, circles the Buddha, and vanishes. That's the whole discourse. It may be the shortest first chapter of any great book. Look back at this week. A warning shouted from a riverbank, the whirlpool ahead. Parents named as first teachers. Effort kept alive in every posture. Word and deed matched, as he speaks, so he does. The short books closed. The Connected Sayings opened, gathered by kind. And now the first of them, back at the water again, with a way across.
screen: `I STOOD STILL AND SANK` · `I PUSHED AND WAS SWEPT AWAY` · `A SWIMMER IN A STRONG RIVER` · `THE DEVA'S VERSE, AND IT VANISHES` · then, large: `NOT HALTING, NOT STRAINING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be a river. Don't stop it, don't push it. When you notice you've drifted off into thoughts, that's halting: gently start moving again by feeling the next breath. When you notice you're gripping, trying hard to breathe well, that's straining: soften the shoulders, the jaw, the belly. Back and forth, finding the place between. Not stuck. Not forcing. Just crossing, one breath at a time. The bell holds the time.
Crossing the flood. The first discourse of the Connected Sayings: the Buddha crossed without halting and without straining, because standing still sinks and pushing gets swept away. Today's word.
Your line: not halting, not straining. Pick one task today you've been either avoiding or forcing, and do ten steady minutes of it, no more, no less. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

fork.reveal: the Buddha says: when I stood still, I sank; when I pushed, I was swept away. the way across was neither.

original.note: Pali ogha: a flood, the current that sweeps beings along.

trapdoor: what you thought: crossing the flood is about a river journey.
what it means: in SN 1.1, the Buddha crossed the flood of craving and confusion by not halting and not straining.

what a scholar hears: elsewhere the canon names four floods, sensual desire, becoming, views and ignorance; SN 1.1 opens the deva-connected chapter, where heavenly beings question the Buddha in verse.
